```{r}
#| label: setup
eff <- read.csv("method-change-effects.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# One value from the CSV; stops unless exactly one row matches.
v <- function(change, quantity, model = NULL, target = NULL, setting = NULL) {
  r <- eff[eff$change == change & eff$quantity == quantity, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!is.null(model))   r <- r[r$model %in% model, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!is.null(target))  r <- r[r$target %in% target, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!is.null(setting)) r <- r[r$setting %in% setting, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(r) != 1L)
    stop(sprintf("v(): %d rows for %s / %s / %s / %s / %s", nrow(r), change, quantity,
                 format(model), format(target), format(setting)))
  r$value
}
num <- function(...) as.numeric(v(...))
# The findings fixes of 6 November 2026 (Sections 3.3 and 3.6), measured by
# 06_findings-effects.R against the package before them.
fe <- read.csv("findings-effects.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
vf <- function(change, quantity, model = NULL, target = NULL, setting = NULL) {
  r <- fe[fe$change == change & fe$quantity == quantity, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!is.null(model))   r <- r[r$model %in% model, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!is.null(target))  r <- r[r$target %in% target, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!is.null(setting)) r <- r[r$setting %in% setting, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(r) != 1L)
    stop(sprintf("vf(): %d rows for %s / %s", nrow(r), change, quantity))
  r$value
}
f2  <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "f", digits = d)
f3  <- function(x) f2(x, 3)
f1  <- function(x) f2(x, 1)
pct <- function(x) paste0(f1(abs(as.numeric(x))), "%")

commit   <- substr(v("meta", "git_sha"), 1, 7)
commit_txt <- paste0(commit, if (identical(v("meta", "git_dirty"), "TRUE"))
  " with uncommitted changes to the package code" else "")

# The approximation gap (Section 3.12), from the Pima script 05_full-space-gap.R.
gap_file <- "../../scripts/paper1-pima/output/full_space_gap.rds"
if (!file.exists(gap_file))
  stop("Run 05_full-space-gap.R first: ", gap_file, " is missing.")
gap <- readRDS(gap_file)
gp_pct <- function(r) paste0(round(100 * (r - 1)), "%")
n_train  <- num("M2", "n_train", model = "4f")
n_test   <- num("M3", "rows_test", model = "4f")
n_g      <- num("M2", "n_minus_g", model = "4f")
row_TP   <- v("meta", "target_row_TP")
row_TN   <- v("meta", "target_row_TN")

run1 <- function(tg, q, setting = "baseline", change = "base") v(change, q, "4f", tg, setting)
words <- function(n) c("no", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six")[as.integer(n) + 1L]
rows_of <- function(change, quantity) eff[eff$change == change & eff$quantity == quantity, ]

n_fixed_runs <- nrow(rows_of("M7", "solution_found"))
n_fixed_none <- sum(rows_of("M7", "solution_found")$value == "FALSE")
ratio_rows   <- eff[eff$change == "M5" & eff$quantity %in% c("ratio_min", "ratio_max"), ]
ratio_relerr <- max(abs(as.numeric(ratio_rows$value) / n_g - 1))
tgt_in <- c(TP = v("M3", "target_global_cf_in_train_ranges", "4f", "TP"),
            TN = v("M3", "target_global_cf_in_train_ranges", "4f", "TN"))
target_range_txt <- if (all(tgt_in == "TRUE")) {
  "The global counterfactuals of both Paper 1 targets lie within the ranges, so their own global distances are the same under either rule; the group medians used to choose them could still move, since the distances of other rows would change."
} else if (all(tgt_in == "FALSE")) {
  "The global counterfactuals of both Paper 1 targets lie outside the ranges, so the thesis rule would have changed their global distances and possibly the choice of targets."
} else {
  sprintf("The global counterfactual of the %s target lies outside the ranges, so the thesis rule would have changed its global distance and possibly the choice of that target.",
          c(TP = "true-positive", TN = "true-negative")[names(tgt_in)[tgt_in == "FALSE"]])
}
sparse_gain  <- c(TP = num("M10", "all_supports_n_changed", target = "TP") -
                    num("M10", "greedy_n_changed", target = "TP"),
                  TN = num("M10", "all_supports_n_changed", target = "TN") -
                    num("M10", "greedy_n_changed", target = "TN"))
```

# Summary {.unnumbered}

This note records the changes made to the method of the thesis (Rowan, 2026) in the `boundarylogic`
package since the thesis was submitted (Sections 2 to 4), and the future work that remains (Section 5).
It separates the **core methodology**, which determines what the method computes, from the **code
improvements** used to implement it, and measures the effect of each change on the Pima diabetes example
of Paper 1 wherever the package can switch the change back.

Eleven core changes are recorded in Section 3. One of them departs from the
thesis text itself, not only from its code: **global counterfactuals outside the training ranges are
kept and reported** rather than discarded (Section 3.3), whereas the thesis filters them (p.93). The
package keeps them so that the distance to the nearest boundary stays correct, at the cost of reporting
some infeasible counterfactuals.

Two other departures were removed on 5 November 2026:

- the comparison of the pairs of components by Mahalanobis rather than Euclidean distance under PCA:
  the package now applies the thesis's rule by projection (p.86), in the pair comparison and in the
  variable importance (Sections 3.1 and 3.5). Paper 1, which uses CVA, is unaffected;
- **the local search without a convex hull**: the package again keeps only the boundary points inside
  the convex hull of the training data on each rotated plane, as the thesis requires (p.117; Section
  3.6). This changes the Phase 3 results of the true-positive target.

On 6 November 2026 two rules were aligned with the text and between the two searches: the hull on each
rotated plane is built from the training data alone, and a closed boundary contour is kept only if it
encloses training data, in the global search (where the rows being searched decided before) and in the
local search (which had no such rule). The Paper 1 results are unchanged (Sections 3.3 and 3.6).

The remaining core changes extend the thesis method (the `"fixed"` and `"integer"` constraints, the
greedy sparse counterfactual, the "No effect" class) or change the scale or reach of a measure (the
within-class standard deviation in the variable importance, the covariance form of $\mathbf{W}$, the cap
on the number of pairs). Section 3.12 adds three properties of the thesis method that the thesis does not
state, all of which the paper relies on, including the measured gap between the distances on the biplot
planes and those in the full space. The code improvements are summarised in Section 4, and Section 5
lists the future work, each item of which Paper 1 names as an area of future improvement.

# How to read this note

**The three baselines.** The *thesis version* of the method is defined by the thesis text (Rowan,
2026, Stellenbosch University, submitted 27 February 2026). Two versions of the thesis code exist and
are reported where they differ from the text or from each other:

- **Appendix A** of the thesis (pp.158–218), which prints the code used for the thesis;
- **the branch `original_PhD_code`** of the package repository, committed on 9 March 2026, after
  submission, as the starting code for the package. Its `*_optimized.R` scripts are not always the same
  as Appendix A.

Where the text, Appendix A and the branch disagree, the text defines the thesis version. Page numbers
are the printed pages of the final thesis, as in the package's other notes.

**The Pima set-up** is that of Paper 1. The `r n_train + n_test` rows without zeros in *Insulin*, *SkinThickness*,
*Glucose* or *BMI* are split 80:20 (seed 121) into `r n_train` training and `r n_test` testing rows. A
generalised additive model (GAM) with a smooth term per feature is fitted to the training data, and the
CVA biplot is built on the four prediction outcomes (TP, TN, FP, FN). Phases 1 and 2 use the seven
features; the global variable importance then drops *DiabetesPedigreeFunction*, *SkinThickness* and
*BMI*, and Phase 3 uses the GAM refitted on *Pregnancies*, *Glucose*, *Insulin* and *Age*. The local
examples use a true positive (test row `r row_TP`) and a true negative (test row `r row_TN`), each the
test row whose global counterfactual distance lies nearest its group's median.

**Measurements.** Every measured number in this note is read from `method-change-effects.csv`, written by the
script `04_method-change-effects.R` at package commit `r commit_txt`, except the approximation gap of
Section 3.12, which `05_full-space-gap.R` measures, and the effects of the changes of 6 November 2026,
which `06_findings-effects.R` measures against the package before them (`findings-effects.csv`). A *toggle* measurement switches one
change back through a package argument and reruns the search; a *stored* measurement reads a
diagnostic the package keeps (for example the search point before a constraint is applied). Changes
that cannot be switched back are described and marked "not measured". Distances are quoted as
$\sqrt{d^2_M}$, the Mahalanobis distance under the package's $\mathbf{W}$ (Section 3.2).

**Proposed paper sentences.** Where a change affects how Paper 1 reports a Pima result, the section
ends with the sentence the paper proposes to use.

# Changes made: core methodology

Table 2 follows the method through its three phases and marks each step as unchanged or changed. The
steps marked as changed are discussed in Sections 3.1 to 3.11; the code-level differences behind the
unchanged steps are listed in Section 4.

| Step | Thesis (text) | Package | Status |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Phase 1** | | | |
| Outlier removal | Optional; none for Pima (p.99), a 90% hull for the loans (p.127) | Optional, off by default: `bl_prepare_data(hull_fraction =)`, on a stand-in projection | Changed (3.11) |
| Projection | PCA or CVA; CVA on the four prediction outcomes (p.92) | `bl_build_projection()` | Unchanged |
| Metric $\mathbf{W}$ | Within-groups SSP (§3.4, p.48) | Within-groups covariance, SSP$/(n-g)$ | Changed (3.2) |
| Decision boundary | Contours at $b \pm \varepsilon$ on a prediction grid (§3.6.1, p.62; $\varepsilon = 0.001$, p.78) | `bl_build_grid(b_margin = 0.001)` | Unchanged |
| Plausibility on the plane | Grid within the convex hull of the training data (p.77) | Hull polygon of the training data | Unchanged |
| **Phase 2** | | | |
| Global counterfactual | Nearest boundary point on the plane, by Euclidean distance (p.75, p.101) | `bl_find_boundary()` | Unchanged |
| Feasibility of the global counterfactual | Training bounds, convex hull, no empty regions (§3.10 step 4, p.93) | Hull and empty-region rules (empty regions judged by the training data); training bounds reported, not applied | Changed (3.3) |
| Re-scoring by the model | Appendix A (pp.183–184) | The same rule | Unchanged |
| Variable importance $T_j$ | Standardised by the overall standard deviation (§4.2.2, p.103) | Within-class standard deviation under CVA; overall standard deviation under PCA | Changed under CVA (3.1) |
| Robustness $R = \sum_j T_j$ | §4.2.3, p.105 | The same sum | Follows 3.1 |
| **Phase 3** | | | |
| Procrustes rotation through the target | First two components of the rotated matrix (§3.5, pp.52–54; p.115) | `.bl_rotate()` | Unchanged (see 3.12) |
| Pairs of components | All $p(p-1)/2$ pairs (p.117) | At most `max_pairs = 21` | Changed (3.4) |

| Actionability | Boundary points filtered by the constraints (p.88) | `set_filters()`, with a `"fixed"` restore | Changed (3.7) |

| Sparse counterfactual | Supporting variables changed, contradicting kept (p.120, p.122) | Greedy, with a stopping rule | Changed (3.10) |

## Variable importance standardised by the within-class standard deviation (CVA)

**Thesis.** The global variable importance decomposes each data point's change vector to its
counterfactual along the variable axes. Each component "is standardised by dividing it by the overall
standard deviation of that variable" (§4.2.2, p.103), and the importance of variable $j$ is the sum of
the absolute standardised components over the data points, $T_j$. The robustness of the model is
$R = \sum_j T_j$ (§4.2.3, p.105). Appendix A and the branch use the total standard deviation of the
training data.

**Package.** Under CVA, `plot.bl_boundary()` and `bl_robustness()` divide each component by the
within-class standard deviation, $\sqrt{W_{jj}}$, by default; `distance = "euclidean"` restores the thesis
version. Under PCA the default has been the thesis's overall standard deviation since 5 November 2026
(`distance = "auto"`); before, the within-class standard deviation was the default for both projections.

**Reason.** The total standard deviation includes the spread between the groups. A variable that
separates the groups well therefore has a large total standard deviation, which shrinks its
standardised distance. This under-weights the variables that matter most for the classification. The
within-class standard deviation measures each component in the same units as the CVA metric.

**Effect on Pima.** The ranking is unchanged on both models, and the thesis rule would have pruned the
same three variables (*`r v("M1", "weakest3", "7f", setting = "total SD")`*). The totals are larger
under the package's rule, with the robustness rising from `r f2(num("M1", "robustness", "7f", setting = "total SD"))`
to `r f2(num("M1", "robustness", "7f", setting = "within-class SD"))` on the seven-feature model.

```{r}
#| label: importance
cols7 <- sub("^total:", "", eff$quantity[eff$change == "M1" & eff$model == "7f" &
                                           grepl("^total:", eff$quantity) &
                                           eff$setting == "total SD"])
imp <- data.frame(
  Variable = cols7,
  `Total SD` = sapply(cols7, function(x) f1(num("M1", paste0("total:", x), "7f", setting = "total SD"))),
  `Rank (total SD)` = sapply(cols7, function(x) v("M1", paste0("rank:", x), "7f", setting = "total SD")),
  `Within-class SD` = sapply(cols7, function(x) f1(num("M1", paste0("total:", x), "7f", setting = "within-class SD"))),
  `Rank (within-class SD)` = sapply(cols7, function(x) v("M1", paste0("rank:", x), "7f", setting = "within-class SD")),
  check.names = FALSE)
imp <- imp[order(as.numeric(imp[["Rank (within-class SD)"]])), ]
knitr::kable(imp, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrr",
             caption = "Table 3. Variable importance totals on the seven-feature model (training rows).")
```

**The Mahalanobis check (Pima issue 9).** The per-variable measure ignores the correlations in
$\mathbf{W}$. Summed over the training rows, the squared per-variable measure exceeds the full squared
Mahalanobis distance by `r pct(v("M1", "mahal_check_pct", "7f"))` on the seven-feature model and by
`r pct(v("M1", "mahal_check_pct", "4f"))` on the four-feature model. *Proposed paper sentence:* "The
per-variable standardisation ignores the correlations between the variables; on the Pima data the
summed squared per-variable distances exceed the full squared Mahalanobis distance by
`r f1(abs(num("M1", "mahal_check_pct", "7f")))`% (seven variables) and
`r f1(abs(num("M1", "mahal_check_pct", "4f")))`% (four variables), so the importance ranks the variables
but does not decompose the distance." A full decomposition is listed in Section 5.

**The importance against the global distances.** The change vector of the thesis lies on the plane,
$\boldsymbol{\delta}_i = (\mathbf{z}_{cf}-\mathbf{z}_i)\mathbf{M}_2^{-}$, and the package keeps it. The
distances `bl_find_boundary()` reports (`dist_x`, `dist_mahalanobis`) measure instead from the observation
itself to its global counterfactual. Since the counterfactual is a point of the plane (Section 3.3), that
gap also resets the part of the observation that lies off the plane, its other $p-2$ canonical
coordinates, to the mean. That part has nothing to do with the boundary and is most of the gap: on the
training rows it is `r pct(100 * num("F3", "offplane_share", "7f"))` of the summed squared global gap on
the seven-feature model and `r pct(100 * num("F3", "offplane_share", "4f"))` on the four-feature model
(within-class standard deviations). The importance and the robustness therefore measure the in-plane
change, as the thesis does, and the global distances are reported only; Paper 1 uses the global
$\sqrt{d^2_M}$ only to choose its two targets.

## The metric W as a covariance matrix

**Thesis.** CVA partitions the total sums of squares and products (SSP) into the between-groups and
within-groups SSP, and $\mathbf{W}$ is the within-groups SSP (§3.4, p.48; p.118), computed on the four
prediction outcomes (p.92). The text also refers to "the common within-group covariance matrix"
(p.84). Appendix A and the branch take biplotEZ's `Wmat`, an SSP with no divisor, invert it with
`solve()`, and use it only to compare the pairs of components.

**Package.** `bl_build_projection()` computes $\mathbf{W}$ as the pooled within-groups covariance, the
SSP divided by $(n-g)$, inverts it with a Cholesky decomposition and stores both. Under CVA it is used by
default in the pair search (Section 3.5) and the variable importance (Section 3.1), and in the
Mahalanobis distances the package reports. Under PCA, $\mathbf{W}$ is computed on the two classes and is
used only when `distance = "mahalanobis"` is passed.

**Reason.** As a covariance, $\mathbf{W}$ measures distances in within-class standard deviations, so
$\sqrt{d^2_M}$ can be read as a number of standard deviations, and $\sqrt{W_{jj}}$ is a standard
deviation that Section 3.1 can use. This also follows the covariance reading on p.84.

**Effect on Pima.** The change is a fixed rescaling. With $n = `r n_train`$ training rows and
$g = `r v("M2", "g_groups", "4f")`$ groups, every squared distance is $n - g = `r n_g`$ times the
thesis value, and every distance is $\sqrt{`r n_g`} = `r f2(num("M2", "sqrt_n_minus_g", "4f"))`$ times
larger. No ranking or selection changes. The distances quoted in Paper 1 are on the package's scale.

## Global counterfactuals outside the training ranges

**Thesis.** The local decision boundaries "are filtered to only contain feasible counterfactuals within
the upper and lower bounds for each feature of the training data", only boundaries within the convex
hull of the training data are considered, and "any local decision boundary area that does not contain
data points is discarded" (§3.10 step 4, p.93). Page 101 is less strict, keeping regions "that contain
training data or fall within the convex hull". The thesis code does not apply the ranges in the global
search: the branch's driver scripts pass no training ranges to it, and instead remove the test rows
that lie outside the training ranges before the search.

**Package.** `bl_find_boundary()` keeps the hull and the empty-region rules: contours are clipped to the
training hull, and a closed contour is kept only if it encloses training rows. Until 6 November 2026 the
rows being searched decided, as in the branch, so one row's counterfactual could depend on which other
rows were searched with it; the training data now decide, so it does not. On Pima no contour or
counterfactual changes (`r vf("M12", "contours_used_after", "4f", setting = "test")` contours on the
four-feature model before and after); on the package's loan example the rule keeps 18 contours
instead of 12 on the four-feature model and moves 346 of its 4,429 global counterfactuals. The package first followed
the thesis text and filtered the boundary points by the training ranges before choosing the nearest one
(13 March 2026, `e42fa03`). Since 24 March 2026 (`ea6a12f`) the ranges are checked after the nearest
point is chosen: points outside them are kept, and only their number is reported in a message, with no
flag on the individual rows. The test rows are also left in place, where the branch removed them.

**Reason.** The change was prompted by a PCA biplot of the iris data. A global counterfactual is a point
on the biplot plane, mapped back to the $p$ features through the two plotted components only:

$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{cf} = \bar{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{z}_{cf}\mathbf{M}_2^{-},$$

where $\mathbf{z}_{cf}$ is the boundary point on the plane, $\mathbf{M}_2^{-}: 2 \times p$ holds the rows
of the inverse projection matrix for the two plotted components, and $\bar{\mathbf{x}}$ is the vector of
training means (on the standardised scale for a standardised PCA biplot). In other words, every
component that is not plotted is set to its mean. The individual feature values of this reconstruction
can therefore fall outside the training ranges, even for a boundary point well inside the convex hull on
the plane. Filtering by the ranges before the selection then discarded the nearest boundary point and
selected a farther one. This changed the distance that the variable importance and the robustness
aggregate, which are meant to measure the distance to the nearest boundary. The package therefore keeps
the nearest point and reports its feasibility.

The commit records that CVA was unaffected. The same reconstruction applies under CVA, however, and the
Pima results below show that counterfactuals on a CVA biplot can also fall outside the training ranges.

**The trade-off.** The two rules trade correct distances against feasibility. Keeping
the nearest point gives the correct distance to the approximated boundary, which the global measures
need, but may report a counterfactual with feature values outside the training data. The thesis rule
reports only feasible counterfactuals, but measures the distance to a farther point, and a data point
may be left without one. A middle course keeps the nearest point for the global measures and flags each
infeasible counterfactual by row, which the package does not yet do; it and the thesis rule as an option
are listed in Section 5.

**Effect on Pima.** Not switchable, so the effect on the importance is not measured. On the
seven-feature model no global counterfactual lies outside the training ranges
(`r v("M3", "cf_outside_train_ranges_train", "7f")` of `r v("M3", "rows_train", "7f")` training rows and
`r v("M3", "cf_outside_train_ranges_test", "7f")` of `r v("M3", "rows_test", "7f")` test rows), so the
pruning is unaffected. On the four-feature model, also a CVA biplot,
`r v("M3", "cf_outside_train_ranges_train", "4f")` of `r v("M3", "rows_train", "4f")` training rows and
`r v("M3", "cf_outside_train_ranges_test", "4f")` of `r v("M3", "rows_test", "4f")` test rows have a
counterfactual outside them; the thesis rule would have replaced these with farther points.
`r target_range_txt` The branch would also have removed
`r v("M3", "test_rows_outside_train_ranges", "7f")` test rows on the seven-feature model before the
search. The local counterfactuals of Paper 1 are unaffected, since the local search applies the training
ranges (Section 3.6).

## A cap on the number of pairs of components

**Thesis.** "the projection matrix is recalculated for all possible two-dimensional biplots formed from
pairs of components", that is $p!/(2!(p-2)!)$ pairs (§4.3.1, p.117). The pair search matters in
practice: the seven-variable Pima counterfactual of the thesis "was created from the biplot generated
by components numbers 1 and 7" (p.118, Figure 4.11), and the true-positive loan example used the second
and fourth components (§5.3.1, p.137).

**Package.** `bl_find_local_cf()` searches the pairs in the order (1,2), (1,3), (2,3), (1,4), …, up to
`max_pairs`. The default was 10 pairs from March to October 2026 and is 21 pairs since 31 October 2026.
Twenty-one pairs cover every pair for $p \le 7$; for eight or more variables the pairs with the highest
components are left out.

**Reason.** Each pair requires a rotation, a prediction grid and a boundary search, so the run time grows
with $p^2$. The earlier cap of 10 would have missed the thesis's own Pima counterfactual: pair (1,7) is
number `r v("M4", "position_of_pair_1_7_in_package_order", "7f")` in the package's order. This is the
reason the cap was raised.

**Effect on Pima.** The four-feature model has `r v("M4", "pairs_available", "4f")` pairs, so a cap of
10 or 21 searches all of them, and the results are identical. The gain of the pair search is measured
instead against pair (1,2) alone (`max_pairs = 1`). Over all pairs, the search distance falls from
`r f2(num("M8", "d_M_search", target = "TP", setting = "run5"))` to
`r f2(num("M8", "d_M_search", target = "TP", setting = "run1"))` for the true positive and from
`r f2(num("M8", "d_M_search", target = "TN", setting = "run5"))` to
`r f2(num("M8", "d_M_search", target = "TN", setting = "run1"))` for the true negative. After the
`"integer"` rounding of Section 3.8, the true positive has no counterfactual on pair (1,2) alone (no
whole number of pregnancies near its search point crosses the boundary), against a reported distance of
`r f2(num("M4", "sqrt_d2M", "4f", "TP", "max_pairs = 21"))` over all pairs; for the true negative the
reported distances are `r f2(num("M4", "sqrt_d2M", "4f", "TN", "max_pairs = 1"))` against
`r f2(num("M4", "sqrt_d2M", "4f", "TN", "max_pairs = 21"))`. The winning pairs are
`r v("M4", "best_pair", "4f", "TP", "max_pairs = 21")` and `r v("M4", "best_pair", "4f", "TN", "max_pairs = 21")`.
With more variables the number of pairs grows quickly (`r v("M4", "pairs_available", "7f")` for seven
variables, `r choose(8, 2)` for eight), so a larger model may need a higher cap, or no cap, to find the nearest
counterfactual. Removing the default cap would return the package to the thesis version.

## The distance that compares the pairs (restored under PCA)

**Thesis.** The counterfactual is "the shortest change vector measured in the full dimensional space
using Euclidean distance for PCA biplots and Mahalanobis distance for CVA biplots" (§3.9.1, p.86), and
the CVA rule is $\min \, \mathbf{d}'\mathbf{W}^{-1}\mathbf{d}$ (p.117). The text also notes that
Euclidean distances on a CVA biplot correspond to Mahalanobis distances in the feature space (p.91).
Appendix A and the branch use the Mahalanobis rule only, and only under CVA.

**Package.** Since 5 November 2026 `bl_find_local_cf()` follows the thesis rule by default
(`distance = "auto"`): Mahalanobis distance under CVA, and under PCA the Euclidean distance in the feature
space with each feature divided by its total standard deviation. Before, Mahalanobis distance was the
default for both projections, and `distance = "euclidean"` compared the pairs by the distance on the
rotated plane.

**Reason.** The default now follows the thesis rule for each projection. Under CVA the package's
Mahalanobis rule agrees with the distance on the plane: its $\mathbf{W}$ makes the rotated
loadings satisfy $\mathbf{V}'\mathbf{W}\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}/(n-g)$, so for a counterfactual on the
plane:

$$d^2_M = (n-g)\, d^2_z,$$

where $d^2_M$ is the squared Mahalanobis distance in the feature space and $d_z$ is the distance on the
rotated plane. In other words, the Mahalanobis rule ranks the pairs as the plane distance does. This
identity is the package's derivation, not the thesis's: with the SSP form of $\mathbf{W}$ in the thesis the
factor is 1. Under a standardised PCA the rotated loadings are orthonormal, so the Euclidean distance in
the feature space equals the plane distance at the search point; measuring it in the feature space also
covers the whole-number candidates of Section 3.8, which lie off the plane.

**Effect on Pima.** Paper 1 uses CVA, so its results are unchanged: the ratio $d^2_M / d^2_z$ equals
$n - g = `r n_g`$ for every pair and both targets, to a relative error below
`r formatC(ratio_relerr, format = "e", digits = 0)`, and the Mahalanobis choice is the pair with the
smallest plane distance for both targets, with and without the `"integer"` constraint (pairs
`r v("M5", "best_pair", "4f", "TP", "run 1 / mahalanobis")` and
`r v("M5", "best_pair", "4f", "TN", "run 1 / mahalanobis")`).

On a PCA biplot of the same four-feature model, outside Paper 1's set-up, the two rules differ. For the
true positive the thesis rule selects pair `r v("M5P", "best_pair", "4f", "TP", "run 1 / euclidean (auto)")`
(distance `r f2(num("M5P", "sqrt_d2M", "4f", "TP", "run 1 / euclidean (auto)"))`), while the earlier
Mahalanobis default finds no whole-number counterfactual; for the true negative the rules select
`r v("M5P", "best_pair", "4f", "TN", "run 1 / euclidean (auto)")` and
`r v("M5P", "best_pair", "4f", "TN", "run 1 / mahalanobis")`. Over the
`r v("M5P", "sweep_test_rows", "4f")` test rows the two rules choose different pairs for
`r v("M5P", "sweep_rows_pair_differs", "4f")`. On the seven-feature PCA biplot the two standardisations of
Section 3.1 rank the variables differently but identify the same three weakest.

## The convex hull in the local search (restored)

**Thesis.** "The counterfactual must be selected from a local decision boundary that is within the
convex hull of the training data" (§4.3.1, p.117), which ensures plausibility (p.116). The hull is
dropped only when an unconstrained solution is acceptable (p.115). Appendix A rebuilds the hull on each
rotated plane from the target and the training data (pp.207, 209); the branch builds it from the target
and the test data, and keeps a closed contour only if it encloses the target.

**Package.** From March to November 2026 `bl_find_local_cf()` applied no hull: the candidate boundary
points were filtered by the actionability constraints and the training ranges only. The recorded reason,
that the rotation invalidates the hull of the global biplot, is correct for that hull, but it does not
cover a hull rebuilt on each rotated plane. Since 5 November 2026 a convex hull is rebuilt on each
rotated plane and only the boundary points inside it are kept, before the other filters
(`set_filters(hull = TRUE)`, the default; `hull = FALSE` gives the earlier search). From 5 to 6 November
the hull was built from the training data and the target, as in Appendix A; since 6 November 2026 it is
built from the training data alone, as the text says, and a contour that is still closed after the clip
is kept only if it encloses training data on the plane, the empty-region rule of the global search
(Section 3.3; the thesis states it for the decision boundaries in general, §3.10 step 4, p.93). Since 6 November 2026 `set_filters()` holds the switches for all three of the thesis's
rules (actionability, feasibility and plausibility, p.116): `train_ranges = FALSE` drops the training
ranges, and both switches off give the unconstrained counterfactual (p.115). A search without a filter
object keeps both rules.

**Reason.** The text requires the hull for plausibility, and Appendix A builds it on each rotated
plane; the earlier reason did not cover such a hull. The hull is the training data's alone, so the
region a counterfactual may come from does not grow with a target that lies outside the training data,
and the empty-region rule is the same in both searches, judged on the same data.

**Effect on Pima.** The true negative is unchanged in every run. The true positive's search moves from
pair `r v("M6", "best_pair", "4f", "TP", "run1 / no hull")` to
`r v("M6", "best_pair", "4f", "TP", "run1 / hull")`, and its search distance from
`r f2(num("M6", "d_M_search", "4f", "TP", "run1 / no hull"))` to
`r f2(num("M6", "d_M_search", "4f", "TP", "run1 / hull"))`: without the hull its counterfactual raised
*Age* from `r v("target", "x_obs:Age", "4f", "TP")` to
`r f2(num("M6", "B_x:Age", "4f", "TP", "run1 / no hull"))`, a point outside the training data on its
plane, while inside the hull it lowers *Age* to `r f2(run1("TP", "B_x:Age"))`. Every true-positive
counterfactual inside the hull lowers *Age*, so the runs that keep *Age* from falling (runs 2, 3 and 4)
have no counterfactual; run 4 had one without the hull. Over the
`r v("M6", "sweep_test_rows", "4f")` test rows (run 1), every row keeps a counterfactual:
`r v("M6", "sweep_unchanged", "4f")` are unchanged and `r v("M6", "sweep_moved", "4f")` move, with
a median search distance `r pct(100 * (num("M6", "sweep_moved_median_ratio", "4f") - 1))` longer
among the moved rows. See the package's `documentation/local-convex-hull.md`.

*The changes of 6 November* (measured by `06_findings-effects.R` against the package before them) leave
every run of both targets unchanged. Over the `r vf("M13", "sweep_test_rows", "4f")` test rows (run 1),
every row keeps a counterfactual and `r vf("M13", "sweep_changed", "4f")` move (test rows
`r vf("M13", "sweep_moved_rows", "4f")`), with a median distance
`r pct(100 * (as.numeric(vf("M13", "sweep_moved_median_ratio", "4f")) - 1))` longer. On the package's
loan example the empty-region rule moves the harness target's constrained counterfactual (an empty
closed contour held its nearest boundary point), and the training-only hull moves the counterfactual of
an applicant who lies outside the training data.

**A constraint that does not bind (Pima issue 5).** With *Pregnancies* and *Age* not allowed to
decrease (run 2), the true negative's counterfactual equals the unconstrained one, because its
unconstrained counterfactual already increases these variables. The true positive's unconstrained
counterfactual lowers both, so the constraint leaves it without a counterfactual. *Proposed paper sentence:*
"A directional constraint changes the counterfactual only when it opposes the unconstrained move; for
the true negative the unconstrained counterfactual already increases *Pregnancies* and *Age*, so the
constraint does not bind."

**Plausibility against actionability (Pima issue 11).** Inside the convex hull, the true
positive (prediction `r f3(num("target", "pred_prob", "4f", "TP"))`) reaches the boundary by lowering
every variable: *Pregnancies* from `r v("target", "x_obs:Pregnancies", "4f", "TP")` to
`r f2(run1("TP", "B_x:Pregnancies"), 0)`, *Glucose* from `r v("target", "x_obs:Glucose", "4f", "TP")`
to `r f2(run1("TP", "B_x:Glucose"))`, *Insulin* from `r v("target", "x_obs:Insulin", "4f", "TP")` to
`r f2(run1("TP", "B_x:Insulin"))` and *Age* from `r v("target", "x_obs:Age", "4f", "TP")` to
`r f2(run1("TP", "B_x:Age"))`. Without the hull it raised *Age* to
`r f2(num("M6", "B_x:Age", "4f", "TP", "run1 / no hull"))`, where the GAM's non-monotone smooth of
*Age* (effective degrees of freedom `r f1(num("I11", "edf:s(Age)", "4f"))`) predicts a lower risk but
only `r v("I11", "train_age_over_50", "4f")` of the `r v("I11", "train_rows", "4f")` training patients
are older than 50. *Proposed paper sentence:* "Without the plausibility rule, the nearest counterfactual for
the true positive raised *Age* from `r v("target", "x_obs:Age", "4f", "TP")` to
`r f1(num("M6", "B_x:Age", "4f", "TP", "run1 / no hull"))`, outside the training data; inside the
convex hull every counterfactual lowers *Age*, which is not actionable, so the constrained runs report
none."

## Fixed variables: a search tolerance and a strict restore

**Thesis.** Two approaches are described (§3.9.2, p.88): building the biplot from the actionable
variables only, with the others fixed at the target's values, or building it on all the data and
filtering the boundary points by the constraints. The examples use the second approach, and a variable
that must not change is held in the sparse counterfactual: "the biplot cannot identify counterfactual
solutions that are precisely whole numbers. This is required to ensure both Pregnancies and Age remain
unchanged" (p.119), and "The number of Pregnancies can remain unchanged" (p.122).

**Package.** `set_filters(tgt, x = "fixed")` lets the search accept a boundary point that moves the
variable by up to 0.5 model units, since a point on a 2D boundary rarely holds a variable exactly. After
the search, `.restore_fixed()` sets each fixed variable back to its observed value and re-scores the
point. If the restored point no longer crosses the boundary, no counterfactual is reported (strict since
4 November 2026), and the message says that changing the constraints on the other variables may make
one possible.

**Reason.** A reported counterfactual must hold every fixed variable exactly, which the thesis achieved
only in the sparse counterfactual.

**Effect on Pima (issue 12).** With *Pregnancies* and *Age* fixed (run 3), and with *Pregnancies* fixed
and *Age* not allowed to decrease (run 4), the true positive has no boundary point within the tolerance
and inside the hull on any of the `r v("M4", "pairs_available", "4f")` pairs (Section 3.6: every
true-positive counterfactual inside the hull lowers *Age*). For the true negative the restored points
score `r f3(num("M7", "B_pred_restored", target = "TN", setting = "run3"))` (run 3) and
`r f3(num("M7", "B_pred_restored", target = "TN", setting = "run4"))` (run 4), which do not cross, so
neither run reports a counterfactual. With *Pregnancies* fixed and *Glucose* not allowed to increase
(run 7), the true-negative search moves *Pregnancies* from
`r v("M7", "observed:Pregnancies", target = "TN", setting = "run7")` to
`r f2(num("M7", "search_value:Pregnancies", target = "TN", setting = "run7"))`; restoring it changes
the prediction from `r f3(num("M7", "B_pred_search", target = "TN", setting = "run7"))` to
`r f3(num("M7", "B_pred_restored", target = "TN", setting = "run7"))`, which still crosses, so the
counterfactual is kept. The true positive's run 7 restore fails
(`r f3(num("M7", "B_pred_restored", target = "TP", setting = "run7"))`). *Proposed paper sentence:*
"When variables are held fixed, the two-dimensional search rarely finds a boundary point that also
holds them; `r words(n_fixed_none)` of the `r words(n_fixed_runs)` runs with a fixed variable report no
counterfactual." A follow-up search that holds the fixed variables exactly is listed in Section 5.

## Whole-number variables: the integer constraint

**Thesis.** "Integer data is included as a continuous variable data type" (p.87), and the biplot
"cannot identify counterfactual solutions that are precisely whole numbers" (p.119).

**Package.** `set_filters(tgt, x = "integer")` rounds the counterfactual after the search. Each moved
integer variable is tried at the whole values just below and above (in raw units); the combinations
that still cross the boundary and meet every constraint and the training ranges are kept, and the
nearest by the search's distance is taken. If none is valid, no counterfactual is reported. This replaces
an earlier rounding of the sparse counterfactual (`round_to`), which rounded in model units without a
re-check.

**Reason.** A count such as *Pregnancies* can only change in whole steps, so a fractional counterfactual
is not actionable.

**Effect on Pima (issue 13).** For the true negative, the search point has *Pregnancies*
`r f2(num("M8", "search_value:Pregnancies", target = "TN", setting = "run1"))`. The value
`r v("target", "x_obs:Pregnancies", "4f", "TN")` does not cross the boundary, so
`r v("M8", "rounded_value:Pregnancies", target = "TN", setting = "run1")` is taken: the distance rises
from `r f2(num("M8", "d_M_search", target = "TN", setting = "run1"))` to
`r f2(num("M8", "d_M_rounded", target = "TN", setting = "run1"))` and the prediction from
`r f3(num("M8", "B_pred_search", target = "TN", setting = "run1"))` to
`r f3(num("M8", "B_pred_rounded", target = "TN", setting = "run1"))`. For the true positive the rounding
moves *Pregnancies* from `r f2(num("M8", "search_value:Pregnancies", target = "TP", setting = "run1"))`
to `r v("M8", "rounded_value:Pregnancies", target = "TP", setting = "run1")` and the distance falls from
`r f2(num("M8", "d_M_search", target = "TP", setting = "run1"))` to
`r f2(num("M8", "d_M_rounded", target = "TP", setting = "run1"))`. *Proposed paper sentence:* "A count
variable can only change in whole steps, so the nearest valid counterfactual may lie well past the
boundary; for the true negative, the whole pregnancy raises the distance from
`r f2(num("M8", "d_M_search", target = "TN", setting = "run1"))` to
`r f2(num("M8", "d_M_rounded", target = "TN", setting = "run1"))`." Letting the other variables
compensate after the rounding is listed in Section 5.

## A "No effect" class for zero Shapley values

**Thesis.** A variable *supports* the counterfactual when its Shapley value moves the prediction towards
the boundary and *contradicts* it otherwise (pp.119–120); variables with no impact can be excluded
from the explanation (p.92). Appendix A counts a value of exactly zero as Supports for a class-0 target
and as Contradicts for a class-1 target (p.216).

**Package.** `bl_shapley()` labels a value with $|\phi_j| < 10^{-8}$ "No effect", and
`bl_find_sparse_cf()` keeps such a variable at its observed value.

**Reason.** A variable whose change never moves the prediction should not be changed in the sparse
counterfactual. This follows the thesis text, which the code's labelling did not.

**Effect on Pima.** "No effect" occurs only where *Pregnancies* ends at its observed value: the true
negative's run 7, after the restore. The true negative is a class-0 target, so Appendix A would have
labelled it Supports, and the sparse counterfactual is the same under both rules.

## The sparse counterfactual: a greedy rule with a stopping point

**Thesis.** "only changing the variables with combined Shapley values equal to the change needed"
reduces the distance and the number of variables (p.120). The Pima example changes *BMI*, *Glucose*,
*Insulin* and *Age* and keeps *Pregnancies* (p.122). No stopping rule is given; in Appendix A the
variables to change are chosen by hand (p.218).

**Package.** `bl_find_sparse_cf()` takes the Supports variables in decreasing order of $|\phi_j|$,
changes one at a time to its counterfactual value, re-scores the point, and stops at the first point
that crosses the boundary. The path is stored. Until 30 October 2026 the package changed all Supports
variables at once.

**Reason.** The Shapley values add up to the full change only at the full counterfactual, so a subset
must be re-scored. This rule is reproducible and gives the shortest prefix of the ranked
Supports variables that changes the class.

**Effect on Pima.** For the true positive, the greedy rule changes
`r v("M10", "greedy_n_changed", target = "TP")` variables (*`r v("M10", "greedy_vars", target = "TP")`*,
prediction `r f3(num("M10", "greedy_pred", target = "TP"))`), against
`r v("M10", "all_supports_n_changed", target = "TP")` when every Supports variable changes (prediction
`r f3(num("M10", "all_supports_pred", target = "TP"))`). For the true negative it changes
`r v("M10", "greedy_n_changed", target = "TN")` (prediction
`r f3(num("M10", "greedy_pred", target = "TN"))`) against
`r v("M10", "all_supports_n_changed", target = "TN")` (prediction
`r f3(num("M10", "all_supports_pred", target = "TN"))`). Both versions cross the boundary for both
targets. For the true positive every Supports variable is needed, so the two rules agree; for the true
negative the greedy rule is sparser by `r words(sparse_gain[["TN"]])` variable.

## Outlier removal before the projection

**Thesis.** Outlier removal is optional. "No outlier data is removed" in the Pima example (p.99); in the
loan example "all data points lying outside the 90% convex hull of the training data were removed" and
"the convex hull fraction was adjusted" (p.127). Appendix A computes the hull on the training biplot
itself.

**Package.** `bl_prepare_data(hull_fraction = )` removes the training rows outside a convex hull that
encloses the given fraction of them, computing the hull on a two-component PCA of the standardised
training features, before the model is fitted. The test data is never filtered. The default was 0.9
from March to November 2026; since 5 November 2026 it is 1, which removes nothing, so outlier removal
is optional, as in the thesis. Each application sets its own value: the loan harness and vignette use
0.9, as the thesis's loan example does, and the Pima example of Paper 1 uses 1, as the thesis's Pima
example does.

**Reason.** The filter runs as part of the data preparation, before the model and the final projection
exist, so it uses a stand-in projection. A value below 1 is worth choosing when extreme training rows
would stretch the biplot and its prediction grid; the default keeps the data as given.

**Effect on Pima.** None: Paper 1 sets `hull_fraction = 1`, which is now also the default. Not
measured.

## Three properties the thesis does not state

These properties are unchanged from the thesis, but Paper 1 relies on them, so they are recorded here.

**Components beyond the canonical dimensions.** With $g$ groups, CVA has
$K = \min(g - 1, p)$ non-zero eigenvalues (§3.4, p.49), so $K = `r v("P212", "K_nonzero_eigenvalues", "4f")`$
for the four prediction outcomes. The remaining $p - K$ components span the null space of the between-groups matrix. When that space has
two or more dimensions, its basis is not unique and is set by the numerical routine; this holds for the
seven-feature model ($p - K = `r v("P212", "p_minus_K", "7f")`$), where the thesis's pair (1,7) uses such
a component. On the four-feature model of Paper 1, $p - K = `r v("P212", "p_minus_K", "4f")`$, so the
fourth component is fixed up to its sign. Both counterfactuals use it (pairs
`r v("P212", "best_pair", target = "TP", setting = "run1")` and
`r v("P212", "best_pair", target = "TN", setting = "run1")`).

**The rotation is not unique.** The Procrustes rotation aligns the plane with a single target point, so
the cross-product matrix has rank 1. This fixes the direction of the target, but the second direction
of the plane is left to a numerical tie-break. The thesis does not discuss this (§3.5, pp.52–54); it
is inherited from the thesis code and documented in the package's rotation note (§4.1). The results are
deterministic for identical inputs, but a perturbation of the loadings at machine precision can move
the plane. On Pima, ordering the CVA groups as the thesis code did changes the loadings by no more than
`r formatC(num("K3", "max_abs_V_difference", "4f"), format = "e", digits = 1)`, yet the true positive
loses its counterfactual: its search point moves, and no whole number of pregnancies near the new point
crosses the boundary (against pair `r run1("TP", "best_pair")` and distance
`r f2(run1("TP", "sqrt_d2M"))` with the package's order). A deterministic replacement is proposed in
Section 5.

**The reported distance is an upper bound (the approximation gap).** The counterfactual is the nearest
boundary point within the planes that are searched, so its distance is at least the distance to the
nearest point of the decision boundary in the full space of the four variables. A constrained search in
the full space measures the gap: for each of the `r gap$hull$n_rows` test rows, the smallest
Mahalanobis distance at which the GAM's probability equals 0.5 within the training ranges, found by a
gradient-based solver from the package's point and from `r gap$n_dirs` random directions. The
package's search distance is a median `r f2(gap$hull$median)` times the full-space distance
(quartiles `r f2(gap$hull$q1)` and `r f2(gap$hull$q3)`, range `r f2(gap$hull$min)` to
`r f2(gap$hull$max)`), and within 5% of it for `r round(100 * gap$hull$share_le_1.05)`% of the rows.
For the two examples the ratios are `r f2(gap$targets$TP$hull$ratio)` (true positive) and
`r f2(gap$targets$TN$hull$ratio)` (true negative). `r gap$hull$n_full_in_train_hull` of the
full-space points lie inside the convex hull of the training data in four dimensions, and their median
ratio is `r f2(gap$hull$median_plausible)`, so the gap is not explained by implausible full-space points.
*Proposed paper sentence:* "The biplot search finds a boundary point a median `r gp_pct(gap$hull$median)`
further from the target than the nearest boundary point in the full four-dimensional space, so the
distances it reports are upper bounds (quartiles `r gp_pct(gap$hull$q1)` and
`r gp_pct(gap$hull$q3)` further)."

# Changes made: code improvements

These changes alter how the method is computed, its default parameters or its numerical behaviour, not
what it computes. Table 4 summarises them with their measured effect on Pima. Run 1 is the paper's
unconstrained run (*Pregnancies* `"integer"`).

| Item | Thesis code → package | Why | Effect on Pima |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Contour band and prediction rounding | $\varepsilon = 0.01$ and predictions floored to 2 decimals → $\varepsilon = 0.001$ (as in the text, p.78) and 3 decimals | Separate the band from the rounding; a narrower band | With $\varepsilon = 0.01$: true-positive distance `r f3(run1("TP", "sqrt_d2M", "b_margin", "K1"))` against `r f3(run1("TP", "sqrt_d2M"))`, prediction `r f3(run1("TP", "B_pred", "b_margin", "K1"))` against `r f3(run1("TP", "B_pred"))`; true-negative distance `r f3(run1("TN", "sqrt_d2M", "b_margin", "K1"))` against `r f3(run1("TN", "sqrt_d2M"))`; the target rule picks test row `r v("K1", "rule_target_TP", "4f", setting = "b_margin")` for the true positive (row `r row_TP` at 0.001). The 2-decimal floor cannot be switched back. |
| Global grid hull fraction | 0.9 → 1 | Every training point inside the hull | Run 1 unchanged for both targets; the target rule picks test row `r v("K2", "rule_target_TN", "4f", setting = "outlie")` for the true negative (row `r row_TN` at 1) |
| Order of the CVA groups | TN, FN, FP, TP (colour names) → FN, FP, TN, TP, fixed | Reproducibility | True positive: no counterfactual with the thesis order (no whole-number point), against pair `r run1("TP", "best_pair")` and distance `r f2(run1("TP", "sqrt_d2M"))`; true negative: `r f2(run1("TN", "sqrt_d2M", "thesis_order", "K3"))` against `r f2(run1("TN", "sqrt_d2M"))` (Section 3.12) |
| Inverse of $\mathbf{W}$ | `solve()` → Cholesky, with a ridge fallback | Numerical stability; detects a singular $\mathbf{W}$ | The ridge fallback is not needed on either model |
| Grid probabilities | No clamp → clamped to [0, 1], with a warning, on the global grid (June 2026) and on each local grid (6 Nov 2026) | Out-of-range model outputs gave missing colours, and on a local grid could stop the search | No warning raised |
| The local plot's window | Set by the training data → widened to show a target or counterfactual outside it (6 Nov 2026) | A target outside the training data was not drawn | Display only |
| The two-colour grid of the global plot | Split at 0.5 → at the model's cutoff (6 Nov 2026) | Consistency with the cutoff | Display only; the same at the cutoff of 0.5 |
| Nearest boundary vertex | Appendix A `which.min`; branch random tie-break → the first nearest vertex | Determinism, as the text states (p.92) | Not measured; the scale on the loan data is in the package's tie-break note (§5) |
| Data behind the local plane | Test data and plot bounds → training data, range plus 10% | The training data defines the projection | Not measured |
| Confusion colours | The thesis scheme in every plot except `plot.bl_projection()` → one shared scheme (TP red, TN blue, FP purple, FN orange) | One colour means one outcome in every biplot | Display only |
| A target at the centre of the biplot | No check → a warning (the rotation is undefined there) | The local plane is arbitrary at the centre | No result changes |
| Hull for the global test search | Test-data hull (branch) → training hull | As the text states (p.93) | Not measured |
| Constraint syntax and pair order | Free expressions; pairs in `combn` order → named forms (`"increase"`, `"decrease"`, ranges); pairs by the second component | Usability | Only ties are affected |
| New diagnostics | None → Mahalanobis distance in the global search; the Phase 2 Mahalanobis check | Reporting | No search result changes |
| Minor items | Grid size; the source of the cutoff; the fallback when no boundary is found; the order of the filters; the Shapley permutation seed ($p > 14$ only); centring on the filtered data; a pair without a boundary point is skipped; PCA allowed in the local search; empty CVA groups dropped | | No effect on the Pima results |

: Table 4. Code improvements and their effect on Pima.

**Bug fixes.** One line each:

- `.bl_rotate()` returned the wrong two columns for pairs other than (1,2), placing the target at the
  origin; fixed on 23 May 2026, restoring the thesis behaviour.
- Task A: two internal helpers switched the user's active graphics device.
- Task B: the local plot coloured the target by another observation's class when the target came from
  a data frame other than the test data.
- Gate 2:
  - fixed variables were marked as used in the sparse counterfactual;
  - the local plots accepted a rotation that misplaced the sparse counterfactual;
  - the grid cutoff was not checked against the model's;
  - models from `xgboost::xgboost()` were rejected;
  - empty CVA groups were coloured wrongly;
  - raw-unit data could be passed to functions that expect model units (`bl_apply_scaling()` and a
    warning were added);
  - the Shapley labels read "observed -> change".

**Future work.** The open items that bear on the method are listed in Section 5.

# Future work

None of these is implemented. Each is left as future work, and Paper 1 names it as an area of future
improvement. Table 5 summarises them; each is described below.

| Change | Why | Expected effect on results | Effort | Decision |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Minimal rotation with a search over planes | Makes the plane unique (Section 3.12) | Moves every Phase 3 result | High | Future work, after Paper 1 |
| A check on other platforms | The plane depends on the linear algebra routine (Section 3.12) | Tests whether the results reproduce | Low | Future work; Paper 1 states its platform |
| Follow-up searches for `"fixed"` and `"integer"`, and a search in the actionable variables only | Fewer runs without a counterfactual; smaller rounding cost | Changes constrained runs only | Medium to high | Future work |
| Feasibility as a constraint inside the search | Finds the nearest feasible point directly | Changes constrained runs | Medium | Future work |
| A configurable `"fixed"` tolerance | The 0.5 tolerance is hard-coded | None at the default | Low | Future work |
| A per-row feasibility flag, and the training-range filter as an option, in the global search | Shows which counterfactuals are infeasible; offers the text's rule (Section 3.3) | None at the default | Low | Future work |
| Storing every pair's plane | Shows the search across planes; allows a failed restore to be retried on the next-best pair | None | Low to medium | Future work |
| Full Mahalanobis decomposition in Phase 2 | Removes the gap of Section 3.1 | Changes the importance values | Medium | Future work |
| Aggregated Shapley values | Global importance from local attributions (thesis §6.2) | New output | High | Future work |
| CVA biplot for a singular $\mathbf{W}$ ($p > n$) | Wide data | New capability | Medium to high | Future work |
| Multi-class models | One boundary for each pair of classes | New capability | High | Future work, a key area |
| A different transformation per variable | Skewed or mixed-scale variables (display only) | None | Medium | Future work |

: Table 5. Possible future changes.

**Minimal rotation with a search over planes.** The package's rotation note (§5) proposes a closed-form
minimal (Givens) rotation that carries the plane onto the target, followed by a reproducible search over
the family of planes that contain the target. This removes the tie-break of Section 3.12 and broadens
the search beyond fixed pairs, in the spirit of the grand tour proposed in the thesis (§6.3, p.144).
Since every Phase 3 number would move, the change should follow Paper 1.

**A check on other platforms.** The Procrustes rotation leaves the plane's second direction to the
linear algebra routine (Section 3.12), so another operating system or linear algebra library may select
a different plane, and hence a different counterfactual. The package has been run on one platform (R
4.6.0 on Windows); Paper 1 states this, and its supplement records the session information. Rerunning the
Pima example on other platforms would test whether its results reproduce; the minimal rotation above
would remove the dependence.

**Follow-up searches for `"fixed"` and `"integer"`.** When the restore of a fixed variable fails, a
second search could move the free variables along the search direction, with the fixed variables held
exactly, until the model crosses the boundary; building the local biplot in the actionable variables
only is the larger alternative. After an integer rounding, the other variables could compensate,
reducing the distance cost of Section 3.8, and a step size other than 1 could be allowed.

**Feasibility as a constraint inside the search.** The constraints and the training ranges filter the
vertices of the boundary contour, so the nearest feasible point may lie between two vertices. Treating
feasibility as a constraint inside the search would find it directly.

**A configurable `"fixed"` tolerance and the global training ranges.** The 0.5 tolerance suits
variables measured in whole units, but not variables on a small scale. For the global search, a flag on
each counterfactual outside the training ranges would show which rows are affected, since the package
reports only their number. An option to filter by the ranges before the selection would offer the thesis
version of Section 3.3 without changing the default.

**Storing every pair's plane.** Only the winning plane is kept, so the other candidates cannot be drawn.
Storing all planes would allow a figure of the search across planes, and the restore of a fixed
variable to be retried on the next-best pair, without changing any other result.

**Full Mahalanobis decomposition in Phase 2.** A Shapley decomposition of the full Mahalanobis distance
would attribute the correlated part of the distance that the per-variable measure ignores. Its cost
grows with $2^p$ per data point.

**Aggregated Shapley values.** The thesis proposes a global importance measure that aggregates the
Shapley contributions over a representative set of data points (§6.2, p.143). This needs a rotation and
a Shapley computation for each data point.

**A CVA biplot for a singular $\mathbf{W}$.** When $p > n$, $\mathbf{W}$ is singular. The generalised
singular value decomposition of Ganey & Gardner-Lubbe (2026, *Statistical Methods & Applications* 35,
825–847; R package `wideRhino`) gives a CVA biplot in this case.

**Multi-class models.** The method explains binary classifiers. A multi-class model can be explained
one class at a time, by coding the class of interest as 1 and the other classes as 0, so that the
counterfactual moves the observation out of that class rather than towards a specific other class. The
CVA biplot already separates more than two groups (here the four outcome groups), so extending the
boundaries and the search to one boundary for each pair of classes, for example through linear
discriminant analysis, is a key area of future research.

**A different transformation per variable.** The package records one affine scaling for display. Allowing
a different transformation for each variable (z-score, log, none) would help skewed variables. A
non-affine transformation needs calibrated non-linear axes, such as the spline-based biplots of
Groenen, le Roux & Gardner-Lubbe (2015, *Advances in Data Analysis and Classification* 9, 219–238).


# Reproduction {.unnumbered}

The measurements were made at package commit `r commit_txt` (`boundarylogic` `r v("meta", "package_version")`,
`r v("meta", "r_version")`, mgcv `r v("meta", "mgcv_version")`, run `r v("meta", "time")`). The scripts
of the Pima example are kept outside the package repository. From that folder:

1. `Rscript run_all.R` builds the data, the models and the Paper 1 results;
2. `Rscript 04_method-change-effects.R` reruns the searches with each change switched back and writes
   `method-change-effects.csv` to this folder; it stops if the baseline does not reproduce the Paper 1
   results;
3. `Rscript 05_full-space-gap.R` measures the approximation gap of Section 3.12;
4. `Rscript 06_findings-effects.R` compares the package before the changes of 6 November 2026 (commit
   `r vf("meta", "before_sha")`, exported from git) with the current one and writes
   `findings-effects.csv` to this folder;
5. `quarto render methodology-changes.qmd --to docx` renders this note.
